name: Grace Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a health insurer, processing medical claims and pre-approvals, so a hospital asks if we'll cover a knee operation or an MRI scan and I check the policy and the doctor's notes. I work from home three days and go into the office in the city centre on Tuesdays and Thursdays. I get through maybe sixty cases a day. I use AI tools all day long; I've set up my own prompts for reading the medical notes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters; a yes from me means someone gets their hip done. I like tinkering with the tools to make my day faster, and my team leader has started asking me to show others. What gets to me is the refusals, especially when the policy wording is unfair but clear. I share a flat with my friend Lou, who's a barista, and I complain to her about it most evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, gently, because I always thought the hype was ahead of the tools. Online I'd post something about how the useful bits are small but real. At work I'd keep showing people my shortcuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for me. I built myself a little AI checklist for knee surgery claims, and it saves me maybe twenty minutes a day. Twenty minutes isn't a revolution, it's a longer lunch. My job stays, my pay stays, and I've got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and keep refining my prompts. I'd ask my team leader to make me the go-to person for the tools, maybe with a small pay bump, and I'd ask for that at my review in March. I'd keep saving 150 a month, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by the idea, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this world, even without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit, because our landlord is selling and we might have to move. But there are plenty of flats in the city and Lou and I split everything. It's an annoyance, not a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask for a pay bump for the tools. What if they said no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd keep doing it anyway because I enjoy it, and update my CV with it. Other insurers in the city would want someone who can do that. I'm not scared of looking.

I'd keep showing colleagues my **shortcuts** at work.
think: Her own AI checklist saves about **twenty minutes** a day, nothing more.
Her job, pay and **four months** of savings would stay intact.
do: Keep refining her **prompts** for medical notes.
Ask at the **March review** to be the paid go-to person for tools.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** by the idea.
S0.quote: I built myself a little AI checklist for knee surgery claims, and it saves me maybe twenty minutes a day. Twenty minutes isn't a revolution, it's a longer lunch.
fieldNote: Her main outside pressure is a **landlord selling**, which she treats as an annoyance.
She already sees her **tool skills** as something she can sell elsewhere.
Her calm comes from **confidence** in the local job market, not from denial.

steps.text: Keep refining her AI prompts for reading medical notes
Keep processing about sixty medical cases a day as now
Keep putting 150 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and we need rules for how insurers use it, especially on health. I'd post about who checks the machine when it says no to someone's treatment. I'd tell friends at other insurers to get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my current job shrinks a lot, but I'm one of the people they'd keep to run and check the tools. Somebody has to check whether the machine is turning down cancer scans for the wrong reasons, and I want that somebody to be me. I'm not naive; if they cut half the team I'd still be nervous until the list came out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an online course in data analysis this winter, about 300, evenings. I'd volunteer to test the new claims software before it rolls out, so my name is on it. I'd join the staff union too, because I'd want the job of checking the machine to be a real role with real pay, not an extra task for the same money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a nervous edge. I like change, but not when it's done badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marion, who's 50-odd and still prints the doctor's letters to read them. She's brilliant on the medical side but she won't touch the tools. I'd try to pair up with her, because she knows things the software doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're both excited and joining a union. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not to me. I can like the technology and still not trust the company to share what it saves. Being good with the tools doesn't mean I trust the people buying them.

Join the **staff union** to make checking AI a paid role.
S1.quote: Somebody has to check whether the machine is turning down cancer scans for the wrong reasons, and I want that somebody to be me.
fieldNote: She positions herself as the **human check** on automated health refusals.
She sees **no conflict** between loving the tools and joining a union.
She worries for **Marion**, whose medical knowledge outruns her tool use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for health decisions and there has to be a human signing off on refusals by law. I'd be campaigning for that loudly. With friends I'd be honest that I'm worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it depends almost entirely on one law. A law saying a human must sign off on every medical refusal would keep me employed for a while. Without that law, I'm a very expensive rubber stamp. And robots arriving three years later doesn't help me much, my job is all screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write to my representative and join whatever campaign pushes for human sign-off on health refusals. I'd lift my savings from four months towards six by cutting eating out. I'd also look, quietly, at something hands-on for the three years before robots arrive, maybe healthcare assistant work, since I know the medical language.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but awake. I'd rather be doing something than lying there worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, definitely, Lou and I go out twice a week. Then the gym, I'd run instead. I wouldn't cut my phone or my laptop; I'd need those to keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Healthcare assistant pays less than you earn now. Would you really do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the choice was that or nothing, yes. I'd take a pay cut to be somewhere the robots aren't yet. It'd buy me three years to work out the next move.

fieldNote: Her job security rests on **regulation**, which she'd campaign for herself.
She'd take a **pay cut** to move into hands-on care for three years.
She keeps her **laptop and phone** while cutting everything else, to stay current.

steps.text: Join the campaign for human sign-off on health refusals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get the rules right, so let's not waste it. I'd be the one running lunch-and-learn sessions at work. Online I'd post about where the new jobs are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be okay. Five years is enough for me to stop processing claims and start auditing the software that processes them. That work probably lasts until AGI can audit itself, which I'm not sure anyone can say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the data course and then a short certificate in AI auditing, about 1,200 all in over two years. I'd apply for the model checking team at our insurer or a bigger one by 2028. I'd keep saving and move with Lou to a cheaper flat so I've got more cushion when I switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. Some unease, but it's the good kind that keeps me going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the auditing jobs don't appear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd still have the data skills, and those go into lots of places. I'd also still have the healthcare assistant idea in my back pocket. I don't like having only one plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does moving to a cheaper flat feel like a step back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, Lou would grumble about the commute. But I'd rather have six months saved and a smaller kitchen than the other way round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it well, and I'd want insurers to pay for staff retraining from the savings. I'd be positive in public. People need to hear it's not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd actually change direction. With ten years, I'd train as a nurse. I've spent years reading about other people's operations, and I'd like to be in the room for one. Robots for that kind of work wouldn't come until 2039, and even then, people want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my claims job for two more years while I save, then apply to a nursing degree around 2029, using my medical claims knowledge. I'd keep using AI tools daily because they'll be in hospitals too. I'd look for a part-time health insurer role during the degree, maybe weekend work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, good. It feels like a second chance at a job I'd care about more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for a nursing degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are student loans and some hospitals pay bursaries for older students. I'd have about six months saved by then and Lou's offered I could pay less rent for a while. It'd be tight, but I'm 27, not 50.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think AI would leave nursing alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it'd change the paperwork side for sure, the notes and the charts. But someone still has to hold a scared person's hand before surgery. That's the bit I'd be there for.

Insurers should fund **staff retraining** from what they save.
think: She'd change direction and **train as a nurse**.
Hands-on care robots would come around **2039**, and people still want a person.
do: Keep the **claims job** two more years while saving.

feel: **Good**, like a **second chance** at more meaningful work.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd train as a nurse. I've spent years reading about other people's operations, and I'd like to be in the room for one.
fieldNote: Ten years turns the threat into a **career switch** she wants.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because everything rides on whether a law appears in time. My generation was told to get a desk job because it was safe. Nobody warned us the desk would be the first thing to go. What would help is a law for human sign-off on health refusals, and funded places on nursing and care courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask whether customers would trust it. Patients already hate it when a computer refuses their scan. I think trust might slow this down more than technology does.

headlineQuote: My generation was told to get a desk job because it was safe. Nobody warned us the desk would be the first thing to go.
portrait: Grace, 27, processes **medical claims** for a health insurer and shares a flat with her friend Lou.
She uses AI **every day** and builds her own prompts for medical notes.
She wants to be the **human check** on automated health refusals.
With more time she'd switch to **nursing**; with less she'd fight for a **sign-off law**.
She likes the technology but **doesn't trust** firms to share its gains.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job depends on a **law** arriving in time.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring **human sign-off** on health refusals.
Funded places on **nursing and care** courses.
